title: Foods with more vitamin C than an orange

seo.title: Foods with more vitamin C than an orange
seo.meta_description: Orange provides about 53 mg vitamin C per 100 g, but red bell pepper, kiwi, broccoli, and some berries can match or exceed it.
seo.search_intent: Find foods with more vitamin C than orange and compare amounts by weight and serving.

excerpt: Orange provides about 53 mg vitamin C per 100 g, but it does not lead the ranking. Raw red bell pepper is around 125–130 mg/100 g, kiwi about 90 mg, and raw broccoli close to 89 mg. Cooking can reduce vitamin C, so the state of the food matters as much as its position in a table.
content_html:
Orange is a good vitamin C source, but it is not the most concentrated common food. Its practical strength is that it is easy to eat in a fairly large serving and is usually eaten raw.

Vitamin C per 100 grams and per serving

FoodVitamin C/100 gTypical servingVitamin C/serving
Raw red bell pepper~127 mg75 g~95 mg
Kiwi~93 mg90 g~84 mg
Raw broccoli~89 mg100 g~89 mg
Strawberries~59 mg150 g~89 mg
Orange~53 mg140 g~74 mg

The clearest gap is red bell pepper: gram for gram it provides about 2.4 times as much vitamin C as orange.

Serving size changes the practical ranking

Strawberries only slightly exceed orange per 100 g, but a 150 g bowl can provide close to 90 mg. A large orange can also provide a substantial amount, so concentration alone is not the whole story.

Heat can lower vitamin C

Vitamin C is water-soluble and heat-sensitive. Boiling can reduce it through both degradation and leaching into cooking water. Shorter cooking and steaming generally preserve more than prolonged boiling.

That is why a raw-food ranking should not be copied directly onto heavily cooked vegetables.

Orange is still a strong source

Other foods having more vitamin C does not make orange a poor choice. One fruit can provide around 70 mg or more along with water, fiber, and other plant compounds.

Serving size can reverse a “highest vitamin C” ranking

Vitamin C tables are often ranked per 100 grams, which is useful for scientific comparison but not always how people eat. A guava may be exceptionally concentrated, yet a cup of strawberries or half a large red bell pepper can also deliver a substantial amount in an ordinary serving. Conversely, a herb or chili pepper can look spectacular per 100 grams even though few people eat 100 grams at once. Comparing both concentration and realistic portions gives a much better answer than declaring one universal winner.

Red and yellow bell peppers are among the easiest ways to exceed an orange in a meal because they can be eaten in generous raw portions. Kiwi, strawberries, papaya and guava are other fruit options, while broccoli and Brussels sprouts contribute meaningful vitamin C among vegetables. The exact ranking changes with variety, ripeness, storage and database entry. The useful message is not that oranges are “low” in vitamin C; it is that citrus is only one member of a much wider group of rich foods.

Cooking changes the numbers because vitamin C is water-soluble and sensitive to heat. Long boiling can both degrade the vitamin and move some of it into the cooking water. Shorter steaming, microwaving or stir-frying often retains more, although the amount depends on time, temperature and cut size. If a vegetable is normally eaten cooked, comparing its raw laboratory value with a ready-to-eat orange can overstate what reaches the plate.

Storage matters too. Fresh produce does not hold exactly the same vitamin C content forever after harvest. Time, warmth and repeated cutting can reduce it. Frozen vegetables are not automatically inferior: commercial freezing often happens soon after harvest, although blanching and storage cause some losses. A frozen broccoli side dish can still be a useful source. Fresh versus frozen is therefore less important than the specific food, processing and how long it has been stored.

Whole fruit also offers more than a vitamin C number. Juice can provide the vitamin, but a glass may be consumed quickly and contains less intact fiber than the corresponding whole fruit. Fortified drinks may supply very high amounts, yet that is added vitamin C rather than the natural concentration of the original ingredient. If the goal is simply to meet vitamin C needs, variety across fruits and vegetables is more robust than chasing the single highest food every day.

Season and cultivar add still more variation. A nutrition database usually reports representative values, not a guaranteed milligram count for every individual pepper or strawberry. That is another reason not to treat small ranking differences as exact. If several foods are all rich sources, the practical choice can be based on availability, taste and how much you will actually eat.

The useful takeaway

If the goal is maximum concentration, red bell pepper and kiwi clearly exceed orange. In normal eating, though, several fruits and vegetables across the day make a single champion unnecessary.

faq.question: What food has more vitamin C than an orange?
faq.answer: Raw red bell pepper provides roughly 125–130 mg per 100 g, more than twice the roughly 53 mg in orange.

faq.question: Does kiwi have more vitamin C than orange?
faq.answer: Yes. Kiwi is around 90–95 mg per 100 g compared with about 53 mg in orange.

faq.question: Does cooking destroy vitamin C?
faq.answer: It can reduce it, especially with prolonged heat and boiling in water. Losses depend on time and cooking method.
